newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank warns Europe deficits must be cut more.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank warns Europe deficits must be cut more.

text.p: Germany's Bundesbank warned on Wednesday that European countries still had a long way to go in cutting their budget deficits for European monetary union.
In its 1996 annual report the central bank said that budget deficits in most European countries remained too high, adding this also placed a restriction on growth in the private sector.

Noting that European countries "with the exception of Germany" had made progress in reducing their budget deficits last year, the central bank nonetheless hit out at attempts by some countries to effect only temporary improvements.

"'Balance sheet cosmetics' clearly do not help in the task of consolidation," the central bank said. "They neither create new fiscal policy scope nor strengthen the competitiveness of the private sector," it said in its 1996 annual report.
Sustainability would be essential for those countries entering monetary union, it said.
Countries which wish to join European monetary union at the planned start date in 1999 must reach key economic targets this year in order to qualify for entry.

Most countries are facing serious problems in trimming their budget deficits back to a target level of three percent of gross domestic product. Germany, which notched up a 3.8 percent deficit in 1996, plans to cut this to 2.9 percent.
In its report, the central bank warned that Bonn should make extra efforts to rein in its deficit, as unforeseen events could otherwise endanger the reaching of its budgetary goal.

Prospects for this year's budget already looked less rosy than had been the case last autumn, given that last year's tax receipts came in lower than expected and the recent rise in unemployment, the Bundesbank said.
"It can also not be ruled out that further unexpected burdens on the budget may arise in the course of the year, whether on the income side or on particular types of expenditure," it added.

"In view of this position efforts are needed to achieve further savings," it said, adding that the reduction of the deficit was not only desirable with a view to Germany's qualification for Maastricht.

Urging all countries in the European Union to continue to pursue stability policies, the Bundesbank warned that this could be particularly important for countries which were currently benefiting from speculation they would enter EMU.
Convincing policies would be particularly important for those countries, which have already benefited from convergence trading on bond markets, it added.
Convergence trading has reduced long-term interest rates in countries such as Italy to bring them in line with core EMU countries, it added.

"The countries concerned must concentrate convincingly on a long-term stability policy in order to prevent considerable setbacks in interest rate and exchange rate develoments which could occur in the event that expectations are disappointed," the Bundesbank said.

Such convergence trades have been driven by the expectation that European monetary union will start on time in 1999 with a large group of countries, the Bundesbank said, making no comment on the likelihood of this scenario.
